#Dealing with my Population data by checking their rows,columns,names of the columns i have,head and structure
install.packages("ggplot2")
install.packages("tidyverse")
library(tidyverse)
library(tidyr)
library("ggplot2")



list.files("Data")

(population <- read.csv("D:/AUCA/CO2_MTProject/Data/world_population.csv"))
(co2        <- read.csv("D:/AUCA/CO2_MTProject/Data/CO2_emission.csv"))
(countries  <- read.csv("D:/AUCA/CO2_MTProject/Data/countries-table-selected-columns second.csv"))

dim(population)     
names(population)  
head(population, 5)
tail(population, 10)
str(population)
nrow(population)
ncol(population)

#Then am going to check where I have duplicates rows and how much are they then drop the duplicates if any and check again the new shape

(sum(duplicated(population)))
(population <- population[!duplicated(population), ])
dim(population)
str(population)
#Checking missing values&dealing with them and see if we have some outliers by using boxplot in the quantitative variables and count them plus dealing with them by using Winsorization/capping process.

colSums(is.na(population))
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))     

boxplot(population$X2022.Population, main = "2022 Population")
boxplot(population$Area..km..,       main = "Area (km2)")
boxplot(population$Density..per.km.., main = "Density")
boxplot(population$Growth.Rate,      main = "Growth Rate")
boxplot(population$World.Population.Percentage, main = "World Pop. %")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

population$Growth.Rate<-as.numeric(population$Growth.Rate)
population$X2022.Population<-as.numeric(population$X2022.Population)
length(boxplot.stats(population$Growth.Rate)$out)
length(boxplot.stats(population$X2022.Population)$out)

#q holds the 25% and 75% points; iqr is the distance between them.
#lower and upper are the “normal range” limits that box plots use.
#pmax lifts values below lower up to it, and pmin brings values above upper down to it.

q     <- quantile(population$Growth.Rate, c(0.25, 0.75), na.rm = TRUE)
iqr   <- q[2] - q[1]
lower <- q[1] - 1.5 * iqr
upper <- q[2] + 1.5 * iqr

(population$Growth.Rate.capped <- pmin(pmax(population$Growth.Rate, lower), upper))

boxplot(population$Growth.Rate, population$Growth.Rate.capped, names= c("original","capped"), main = "Comparing the two columns")

#Let's see the growth rate r, time period t, the projection Nt=p*e^(r*t) and round them to the whole people

(population$r <- population$Growth.Rate-1)
(t <- 2030-2022)
(population$Pop2030 <- population$X2022.Population * exp(population$r*t))
(population$Pop2030 <- round(population$Pop2030))
head(population[, c("Country.Territory", "X2022.Population", "r", "Pop2030")], 10)
sum(is.na(population$Pop2030))
summary(population$Pop2030)

#Let's see which country changes most with the biggest increase & decrease

(population$Change <- population$Pop2030 - population$X2022.Population)
head(population[order(-population$Change),c("Country.Territory","Change")], 5)
head(population[order(population$Change),c("Country.Territory","Change")], 5)

# Top ten countries with high population number and their performance during 2022

install.packages("ggplot2")
library(ggplot2)

(top10 <- head(population[order(-population$X2022.Population), ], 10))
top10[, c("Country.Territory","X2022.Population")]

ggplot(top10, aes(x=reorder(Country.Territory, X2022.Population), y=X2022.Population/1e6)) + geom_col(fill="steelblue") + coord_flip() + labs(title= "Top 10 most populous countries, 2022", x="country", y="population(millions)")
ggsave("plot_top10_2022.png", width = 7, height = 5)

# Reshape from wide to long using built-in Base R
(trend <- reshape(top10, 
                 varying = c("X1990.Population", "X2000.Population", 
                             "X2010.Population", "X2015.Population", 
                             "X2020.Population", "X2022.Population"),
                 v.names = "Population",
                 timevar = "Year",
                 times = c(1990, 2000, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2022),
                 direction = "long"))

ggplot2::ggplot(trend, ggplot2::aes(x = Year, y = Population / 1e6, color = Country.Territory)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(size = 1.2) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Population Trends for Top 10 Countries (1990–2022)",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Population (Millions)",
       color = "Country") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()

nrow(trend)                                  
head(trend[, c("Country.Territory", "Year", "Population")], 12)
ggplot2::ggsave("plot_trend_top10.png", width = 8, height = 5)

#Extracting the 10 countries from the CO2 table

(co2_top10 <- co2[co2$country_code %in% top10$CCA3, ])
nrow(co2_top10)                                  
co2_top10[, c("Country.Name", "country_code")]   
rowSums(is.na(co2_top10[, paste0("X", 1990:2019)]))
co2_long <- reshape(co2_top10,
                    direction = "long",
                    varying   = paste0("X", 1990:2019),
                    v.names   = "CO2",
                    timevar   = "Year",
                    times     = 1990:2019,
                    idvar     = "country_code")

nrow(co2_long)   
summary(co2)

ggplot2::ggplot(co2_long, ggplot2::aes(x = Year, y = CO2, color = Country.Name)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "CO2 emissions of the top 10 most populous countries, 1990-2019",
       x = "Year",
       y = "CO2 emissions (metric tons per capita)",
       color = "Country") + ggplot2::theme_minimal() 

ggplot2::ggsave("plot_co2_top10.png", width = 8, height = 5)

#Correlation Analysis

 (vars<-population[,c("Area..km..","Density..per.km..","Growth.Rate","World.Population.Percentage")])
 (names(vars)<-c("Area", "Density", "GrowthRate", "WorldPopPct"))
 head(vars)

(cor_matrix<-round(cor(vars), 2))

library(ggplot2)

(cor_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(cor_matrix)))
(names(cor_long) <- c("Var1", "Var2", "Correlation"))

ggplot(cor_long, aes(x = Var1, y = Var2, fill = Correlation)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = Correlation)) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "white", high = "red",
                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Correlation heatmap of population variables",
       x = "", y = "") +
  theme_minimal()

ggsave("plot_heatmap.png", width = 6, height = 5)
 round(cor(vars,method="spearman"),2)
head(population[order(-population$Density..per.km..),
                c("Country.Territory", "Density..per.km..")], 5)
                
cor_sp <- round(cor(vars, method = "spearman"), 2)
cor_sp_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(cor_sp))
names(cor_sp_long) <- c("Var1", "Var2", "Correlation")

ggplot(cor_sp_long, aes(x = Var1, y = Var2, fill = Correlation)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = Correlation)) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "white", high = "red",
                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Spearman correlation heatmap", x = "", y = "") +
  theme_minimal()

ggsave("plot_heatmap_spearman.png", width = 6, height = 5)

#Merging the Population and CO2 data
sum(population$Country.Territory %in% co2$Country.Name)
(pop2022 <- population[, c("CCA3", "Country.Territory", "Continent", "X2022.Population")])

co2_2019 <- co2[, c("country_code", "Country.Name", "X2019")]
(names(co2_2019) <- c("CCA3", "CO2_Name", "CO2_2019"))

merged <- merge(pop2022, co2_2019, by = "CCA3")

nrow(merged)
head(merged)

colSums(is.na(merged))               
merged <- merged[!is.na(merged$CO2_2019), ]   
nrow(merged)

#Determining the pattern of relationships between population number and CO2 emissions.(Population in millions is more easier to read than pop in billions)

library(ggplot2)
merged$Pop_millions <- merged$X2022.Population / 1e6
summary(merged[, c("Pop_millions", "CO2_2019")])

ggplot(merged, aes(x = Pop_millions, y = CO2_2019)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Population (2022) vs CO2 emissions per capita (2019)",
       x = "Population (millions)",
       y = "CO2 emissions (metric tons per capita)") +
  theme_minimal()

ggsave("plot_scatter.png", width = 7, height = 5)

ggplot(merged, aes(x = Pop_millions, y = CO2_2019)) +
  geom_point(color = "darkblue") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Population (log scale) vs CO2 emissions per capita",
       x = "Population (millions, log scale)",
       y = "CO2 emissions (metric tons per capita)") +
  theme_minimal()

ggsave("plot_scatter_log.png", width = 7, height = 5)

#Pearson, Spearman and Pearson on a log population
cor(merged$Pop_millions, merged$CO2_2019)                        
cor(merged$Pop_millions, merged$CO2_2019, method = "spearman")   
cor(log10(merged$Pop_millions), merged$CO2_2019)                  

#Simple regression

model <- lm(CO2_2019 ~ log10(Pop_millions), data = merged)
summary(model)
cor.test(merged$Pop_millions, merged$CO2_2019, method = "spearman")
#Our P-value shows that our results/relationship is not statistically significant since is greater than 0.05.

merged$CO2_total_Mt <- merged$CO2_2019 * merged$Pop_millions   # million metric tons (approximate)

cor(merged$Pop_millions, merged$CO2_total_Mt)

#CO2 emissions by continent  to and their total emission(metric tons per capita)

continent_co2 <- aggregate(CO2_2019 ~ Continent, data = merged, FUN = sum)
(continent_co2 <- continent_co2[order(-continent_co2$CO2_2019), ])

ggplot(continent_co2, aes(x = reorder(Continent, CO2_2019), y = CO2_2019)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkgreen") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Sum of 2019 CO2 emissions by continent",
       x = "Continent",
       y = "Sum of CO2 emissions (metric tons per capita)") +
  theme_minimal()

ggsave("plot_continent.png", width = 7, height = 5)

table(merged$Continent)
aggregate(CO2_2019 ~ Continent, data = merged, FUN = mean)

merged[which.min(merged$CO2_2019), c("Country.Territory", "CO2_2019")]  
merged[which.max(merged$CO2_2019), c("Country.Territory", "CO2_2019")]  

continent_co2[3, ]
continent_co2[nrow(continent_co2), ]

list.files(pattern = "plot_")

getwd()
